records.title: Project Memory Authority, Lifecycle, and Provenance Foundation
records.question: What controlling policies, authority hierarchy, trust classes, freshness model, and provenance rules should govern Project Memory before any schema, scanner, registry, renderer, or retrieval tool exists?
records.selected_option: ACCEPTED as a parallel governance, documentation, and developer infrastructure workstream. Defined seven-tier authority hierarchy, eight trust classes, commit-bound freshness, supersession, conflicting-evidence resolution, owner-decision representation, generated-evidence requirements, memory-update approval, roadmap synchronization, stale-index behavior, tool provenance, prompt-injection boundaries, branch synchronization policy, and product boundaries.
records.rationale: Without normalized controlling policies, context tools, retrieval systems, agent prompts, and generated indexes could silently drift from the authoritative roadmap and live code.

records.title: Schema and Normalized-Registry Architecture
records.question: What exact data model, schema standard, registry decomposition, stable identifier contract, and validation architecture should Project Memory adopt?
records.selected_option: JSON as canonical tracked registry format; JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 as formal data contract; one schema bundle with typed $defs; 12 separate normalized registry files; registry manifest; dependency-free standard-library validator; tracked source versus generated snapshot separation; stable namespaced identifiers; enforced trust classes, lifecycle values, and cross-record references.
records.rationale: The architecture must support deterministic comparison between plan and implementation, allow later scanners and renderers to extend records without replacing identifiers, and enforce product safety boundaries through structural validation.
